body.text: ye tu tīkṣṇendriyāḥ paṭubuddhayas teṣāṃ punar gaṇanāprayogeṇa priyārohatā bhavati / tatropadiṣṭā evaṃ gaṇanāprayogaṃ laghu laghv eva pratividhyanti, na ca tenābhiramante / te punar āśvāsapraśvāsālambanāṃ smṛtim upanibadhya yatra ca pravartante yāvac ca pravartante, yathā ca pravartante, yadā ca pravartante, tat sarvam anugacchaty upalakṣayaty upasthitayā smṛtyā / ayam evaṃrūpas teṣāṃ prayogaḥ /
body.translated_text: would [overwhelm them]. But for those of sharp faculties and keen intelligence, the practice of counting produces annoyance. For them, once counting has been instructed, [they should proceed to the next stage].

body.text: tasya ca prayogasyāsevanānvayād bhāvanānvayād bahulīkārānvayāt kāyaprasrabdhir utpadyate, cittaprasrabdhiś ca / ekāgratāṃ ca spṛśaty ālambanābhiratiṃ ca nirgacchati //
body.translated_text: Through the repeated practice, cultivation, and frequent application of this practice, bodily tranquility (<s>kāyapraśrabdhi</s>) arises, mental tranquility (<s>cittapraśrabdhi</s>) arises,

body.text:
-II-3-b-(5)-ii-(b) Ms.75b4M, Sh.226-5, W.90-36, P.105a4, D.86a7, N.91a4, Co.91b5, Ch.431c16
sa evaṃ kṛtaparicayo grāhyagrāhakavastumanasikāreṇa skandhān avatarati / kathaṃ ca punar avatarati / ye cāśvāsapraśvāsā yaś caiṣām āśrayakāyas taṃ manasikurvan rūpaskandham avatarati / yā teṣām āśvāsapraśvāsānāṃ tadgrāhikayā smṛtyā saṃprayuktānubhāvanā sa vedanāskandha ity avatarati / yā saṃjānanā sa saṃjñāskandha ity avatarati / yā cāsau smṛtir yā ca cetanā, yā ca tatra prajñā, ayaṃ saṃskāraskandha ity avatarati / yac (

children.translated_text: Śbh II 92

children.text: ) cittaṃ mano vijñānam ayaṃ vijñanaskandha ity avatarati / yā tadbahulavihāritā evaṃ skandheṣv avatīrṇasyāyam ucyate skandhāvatāraparicayaḥ //
children.translated_text: ) mind, thought, consciousness — this is the consciousness-aggregate" — thus one enters [understanding]. The frequent dwelling thus by one who has entered [understanding of] the aggregates — this is called familiarization with the entry into the aggregates.

body.translated_text: Having thus obtained familiarity with counting, one enters the stage of following (<s>anugama</s>).

body.text:
-II-3-b-(5)-ii-(c) Ms.75b6L, Sh.226-17, P.105b1, D.86b3, N.91a7, Co.92a1, Ch.431c26
yadā cānena skandhamātraṃ dṛṣṭaṃ bhavati parijñātaṃ saṃskāramātraṃ vastumātraṃ tadā sa eṣām eva saṃskārāṇāṃ pratītyasamutpādam avatarati / kathaṃ ca punar avatarati / sa evaṃ samanveṣate paryeṣate, "itīma āśvāsapraśvāsāḥ kimāśritāḥ kiṃpratyayāḥ" / tasyaivaṃ bhavati / "kāyāśritā eta āśvāsapraśvāsāḥ kāyapratyayāś cittāśritāś cittapratyayāś ca" /
body.translated_text: When one has seen merely the aggregates, fully known merely the formations, merely the things — then one enters [understanding of] the dependent origination of these very formations. And how does one enter [understanding]? One thus investigates and searches: "Upon what do these in-breaths and out-breaths depend? What is their condition?" One thinks thus: "These in-breaths and out-breaths depend upon the body, are conditioned by the body; they depend upon the mind, are conditioned by the mind."

body.text: "kāyaḥ punaś cittaṃ ca kiṃpratyayaṃ ca / sa "kāyaś cittaṃ ca jīvitendriyapratyayam" ity avatarati / "jīvitendriyaṃ punaḥ kiṃpratyayam" / sa pūrvasaṃskārapratyayaṃ jīvitendriyam ity avatarati /
body.translated_text: "And the body and mind — what is their condition?" One enters [understanding]: "The body and mind are conditioned by the life-faculty." "And what is the condition of the life-faculty?" One enters [understanding]: "The life-faculty is conditioned by previous formations."

body.text: "pūrvakaḥ saṃskāraḥ kiṃpratyayaḥ / sa "pūrvakaḥ saṃskāro 'vidyāpratyaya" ity avatarati / iti hy avidyāpratyayaḥ pūrvakaḥ saṃskāraḥ, pūrvasaṃskārapratyayaṃ jīvitendriyaṃ, jīvitendriyapratyayaḥ kāyaś cittaṃ ca, kāyacittapratyayā āśvāsapraśvāsāḥ / tatrāvidyānirodhāt saṃskāranirodhaḥ / saṃskāranirodhāj jīvitendriyanirodhaḥ / jīvitendriyanirodhāt (

children.translated_text: <s>Śbh</s> II 94

children.text: ) kāyacittanirodhaḥ / kāyacittanirodhād āśvāsapraśvāsanirodhaḥ/ evam asau pratītyasamutpādam avatarati / sa tadbahulavihārī pratītyasamutpādāvatāre kṛtaparicaya ity ucyate / ayam ucyate pratītyasamutpādāvatāraparicayaḥ //
children.translated_text: ) comes the cessation of body and mind; from the cessation of body and mind comes the cessation of in-breaths and out-breaths. Thus one enters [understanding of] dependent origination. One who frequently dwells thus and is familiarized with the entry into dependent origination is called 'one familiarized with the entry into dependent origination.' This is called familiarization with the entry into dependent origination.

body.translated_text: "And what is the condition of the previous formations?" One enters [understanding]: "The previous formations are conditioned by ignorance." Thus: ignorance conditions the previous formations, the previous formations condition the life-faculty, the life-faculty conditions the body and mind, and the body and mind condition the in-breaths and out-breaths. Therein, from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of formations; from the cessation of formations comes the cessation of the life-faculty; from the cessation of the life-faculty,

body.text:
-II-3-b-(5)-ii-(d) Ms.76a1M, Sh.228-1, P.106a2, D.87a2, N.91b7, Co.92a7, Ch.432a12
sa evaṃ pratītyasamutpāde kṛtaparicayo "ya ete saṃskārāḥ pratītyasamutpannā anityā eta" ity avatarati / "anityatvād abhūtvā ca bhavanti bhūtvā prativigacchanti / punar ete 'bhūtvā bhavanti bhūtvā ca prativigacchanti te jātidharmāṇaḥ, jarādharmāṇaḥ, vyādhidharmāṇaḥ, maraṇadharmāṇaḥ / ye jātijarāvyādhimaraṇadharmāṇas te duḥkhāḥ, ye duḥkhās te 'nātmānaḥ, asvatantrāḥ, svāmivirahitāḥ" / evaṃ so 'nityaduḥkhaśūnyānātmākārair duḥkhasatyam avatīrṇo bhavati / tasyaivaṃ bhavati / "yā kācid eṣāṃ saṃskārāṇām abhinirvṛttir duḥkhabhūtā rogabhūtā gaṇḍabhūtā sarvāsau tṛṣṇāpratyayā / yat punar asyā duḥkhajanikāyās tṛṣṇāyā aśeṣaprahāṇam etac chāntam etat praṇītam evaṃ ca me jānata evaṃ bahulavihāriṇas tṛṣṇāyā aśeṣaprahāṇaṃ bhaviṣyatī"ti / evaṃ hi samudayasatyaṃ nirodhasatyaṃ mārgasatyam avatīrṇo bhavati / sa tadbahulavihārī yadā satyāny abhisamāgacchati / ayam asyocyate satyāvatāraparicayaḥ /
body.translated_text: One thus familiarized with dependent origination enters [understanding]: "These formations that are dependently arisen are impermanent." "Being impermanent, they are" [suffering] — thus one enters [understanding].

body.text: tasyaivam satyeṣu kṛtaparicayasya darśanaprahātavyeṣu kleśeṣu prahīṇeṣu bhāvanāprahātavyā avaśiṣṭā bhavanti //
body.translated_text: For one thus familiarized with the truths, the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing are abandoned, and the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation remain.

body.text:
-II-3-b-(5)-ii-(e) Ms.76a4 L, Sh.228-19, P.106b3, D.87b1, N.92a6, Co.92b6, Ch.432a28
yeṣāṃ prahāṇāya ṣoḍaśākāraparicayaṃ karoti / katame punaḥ ṣoḍaśākārāḥ / (

children.translated_text: <s>Śbh</s> II 96

children.text: ) tadyathā smṛta āśvasan "smṛta āśvasimī"ti śikṣate / smṛtaḥ praśvasan "praśvasimī"ti śikṣate / dīrgham hrasvaṃ sarvakāyapratisaṃvedy āśvasan "sarvakāyapratisaṃvedy āśvasimī"ti śikṣate / sarvakāyapratisaṃvedī praśvasan "sarvakāyapratisaṃvedī praśvasimī"ti śikṣate / prasrabhya kāyasaṃskārān āśvasan "prasrabhya kāyasaṃskārān āśvasimī"ti śikṣate / prasrabhyakāyasaṃskārān praśvasan "prasrabhya kāyasaṃskārān praśvasimī"ti śikṣate / prītipratisaṃvedī sukhapratisaṃvedī śikṣate / cittasaṃskārapratisaṃvedī prasrabhya cittasaṃskārān āśvasan "prasrabhya cittasaṃskārān āśvasimī"ti śikṣate / prasrabhya cittasaṃskārān praśvasan "prasrabhya cittasaṃskārān praśvasimī"ti śikṣate / cittapratisaṃvedī / abhipramodayaṃś cittaṃ samādadhaṃś crttaṃ vimocayaṃś cittam āśvasan "vimocayaṃś cittam āśvasimī"ti śikṣate / vimocayaṃś cittaṃ praśvasan "vimocayaṃś cittaṃ praśvasimī"ti śikṣate / anityānudarśī, prahāṇānudarśī, virāgānudarśī, nirodhānudarśy āśvasan "nirodhānudarśy āśvasimī"ti śikṣate / nirodhānudarśī praśvasan nirodhānudarśī praśvasimīti (
children.translated_text: ) Namely: breathing in mindfully, one trains: "I breathe in mindfully." Breathing out mindfully, one trains: "I breathe out mindfully." Breathing in experiencing the whole body — breathing in long, short — one trains: "I breathe in experiencing the whole body." Experiencing the whole body while breathing out,
<s>Śbh</s> II 98
) one trains.

body.translated_text: For the abandonment of which one becomes familiarized with the sixteen aspects. What then are the sixteen aspects?

body.text:
-II-3-b-(5)-ii-(f) Ms.76a7M, Sh.231-9, P.107a7, D.88a3, N.93a1, Co.93a7, Ch.432b28
kaḥ punar eṣāṃ vibhāga ākārāṇām / sa śaikṣo dṛṣṭapado lābhī bhavati caturṇāṃ smṛtyupasthānānām / āśvāsapraśvāsālambanaṃ ca manaskāram ārabhate 'vaśiṣṭānāṃ saṃyojanānāṃ prahāṇāya / tenāha "smṛta āśvasan 'smṛta āśvasimī'ti śikṣate, smṛtaḥ praśvasan 'praśvasimī'ti śikṣate" /
body.translated_text: What then is the division of these aspects? The learner (<s>śaikṣa</s>) who has seen the path obtains the four foundations of mindfulness. Based on the object of in-breaths and out-breaths,

body.text: yadāśvāsaṃ vā praśvāsaṃ vālambate tadā "dīrgham āśvasimi praśvasimī"ti śikṣate /
body.translated_text: when one takes as object the in-breath or the out-breath, then one trains: "I breathe in long" or "I breathe out long."

body.text: yadāntarāśvāsam antarapraśvāsaṃ vālambanīkaroti tadā "hrasvam āśvasimi praśvasimī"ti śikṣate / tathā hy āśvāsapraśvāsā dīrghāḥ pravartante, antarāśvāsā antarapraśvāsāś ca hrasvāḥ / te yathaiva pravartante tathaivopalakṣayati jānāti /
body.translated_text: When one takes as object the intermediate in-breath or the intermediate out-breath, then one trains: "I breathe in short" or "I breathe out short." For the in-breaths and out-breaths proceed as long, while the intermediate in-breaths and intermediate out-breaths are short. As they actually proceed,

body.text: yadā sūkṣmasauṣiryagatān āśvāsapraśvāsān romakūpānupraviṣṭān kāye 'dhimucyate, ālambanīkaroti tadā sarvakāyapratisaṃvedī bhavati /
body.translated_text: when one resolves upon and takes as object the in-breaths and out-breaths that have gone into the subtlety of the pores, having entered the hair-pores of the body — then one experiences the whole body.

body.text: yasmin vā punaḥ samaye niruddha āśvāse 'ntarāśvāse ca / āśvāsapraśvāsaśūnyām āśvāsapraśvāsāpetām avasthām ālambanīkaroti / (

children.translated_text: <s>Śbh</s> II 100

children.text: ) niruddhe ca praśvāse 'ntarapraśvāse ca / anutpanna āśvāse 'ntarāśvāse ca / praśvāsāśvāsaśūnyāṃ tadvyapetāṃ tadvyavahitāṃ riktām avasthām ālambanīkaroti / tasmin samaye prasrabhya kāyasaṃskārān āśvasan, "prasrabhya kāyasaṃskārān āśvasimī"ti śikṣate / prasrabhya kāyasaṃskārān praśvasan, "prasrabhya kāyasaṃskārān praśvasimī"ti śikṣate /
children.translated_text: ) And when the out-breath and intermediate out-breath have ceased, and the in-breath and intermediate in-breath have not yet arisen, one takes as object the state that is devoid of out-breaths and in-breaths, separated from them, interrupted by them, empty. At that time, calming the bodily formations, one breathes in —

body.translated_text: Or again, at the time when the in-breath and intermediate in-breath have ceased, one takes as object the state that is devoid of in-breaths and out-breaths, separated from in-breaths and out-breaths.

body.text: api tu khalu tasyāsevanānvayād bhāvanānvayād bahulīkārānvayāt / ye kharā duḥsaṃsparśā āśvāsapraśvāsāḥ pūrvam akṛtaparicayasya pravṛtta bhavanti / kṛtaparicayasya anye ca mṛdavaḥ sukhasaṃsparśāḥ pravartante / tenāha "prasrabhya kāyasaṃskārān āśvasimīti śikṣate" /
body.translated_text: However, through the continuity of practice, the continuity of cultivation, and the continuity of repeated application — those in-breaths and out-breaths which were coarse and unpleasant to touch for one who was previously unfamiliarized, become, for one who is familiarized, other [breaths that are] gentle and pleasant to touch, and they proceed [thus].

body.text: sa caivam ānāpānasmṛtiprayogeṇa ca yuktaḥ sacel lābhī bhavati prathamasya vā dhyānasya dvitīyasya vā tasmin samaye prītipratisaṃvedy āśvasan, "prītipratisaṃvedy āśvasimī"ti śikṣate /
body.translated_text: And when one thus engaged in the practice of <s>ānāpānasmṛti</s> (mindfulness of breathing) obtains the first or second <s>dhyāna</s> — at that time, experiencing joy while breathing in, one trains: "I breathe in experiencing joy."

body.text: sacet punar lābhī bhavati niṣprītikasya tṛtīyasya dhyānasya sa tasmin samaye sukhapratisaṃvedī bhavati / tṛtīyāc ca dhyānād ūrdhvam ānāpānasmṛtisaṃprayogo nāsti / yena yāvat tṛtīyadhyānāt parikīrtitam saṃgṛhītam /
body.translated_text: If then one obtains the third <s>dhyāna</s>, which is without joy, at that time one experiences happiness. And beyond the third <s>dhyāna</s>, there is no practice connected with mindfulness of breathing. For this reason, it has been taught up to the third <s>dhyāna</s>.

body.text: tasyaivaṃ prītipratisaṃvedino vā sukhapratisaṃvedino vā sacet kadācit karhacit smṛtisaṃpramoṣād utpadyate / "asmī"ti vā, "ayam aham asmī"ti vā, "bhaviṣyāmī"ti vā, "na bhaviṣyāmī"ti vā, "rūpī bhaviṣyāmy arūpī bhaviṣyāmi" (

children.translated_text: <s>Śbh</s> II 102

children.text: ) / "saṃjñī, asaṃjñī, naivasaṃjñīnāsaṃjñī bhaviṣyāmī"ti, evam saṃmohasaṃjñācetanāsahagatam iñjitaṃ manyitaprapañcitābhisaṃskṛtaṃ tṛṣṇāgatam utpadyate / sa tad utpannaṃ laghu laghv eva prajñayā pratividhyati nādhivāsayati prajahāti vinodayati vyantīkaroti / evaṃ cittasaṃskārapratisaṃvedī "prasrabhya cittasaṃskārān āśvasimī"ty āśvasan "prasrabhya cittasaṃskārān āśvasimī"ti śikṣate /
children.translated_text: ) or "I shall be with perception, without perception, or with neither-perception-nor-non-perception" — thus there arises a stirring accompanied by bewilderment, perception, and volition, a conceiving, proliferating, constructing, gone to craving. One quickly, very quickly, with wisdom discerns and penetrates that which has arisen —

body.translated_text: For one thus experiencing joy or experiencing happiness, if at any time whatsoever, through lapse of mindfulness, there arises [the thought]: "I am," or "This I am," or "I shall be," or "I shall not be," or "I shall be with form,"

body.text: sacet punar lābhī bhavati maulānāṃ prathamadvitīyatṛtīyānāṃ dhyānānāṃ sa cāvaśyam anāgamyasya prathamadhyānasāmantakasya lābhī bhavati / sa taṃ niśrityotpannaṃ svaṃ cittaṃ pratyavekṣate / sarāgaṃ vā vigatarāgaṃ vā sadveṣaṃ vā vigatadveṣaṃ vā samohaṃ vigatamohaṃ, saṃkṣiptaṃ vikṣiptaṃ līnaṃ pragṛhītam uddhatam anuddhataṃ vyupaśāntaṃ avyupaśāntaṃ samāhitam asamāhitaṃ subhāvitam asubhāvitaṃ vimuktaṃ cittam avimuktaṃ cittam iti yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti pratisaṃvedayati / tenāha cittapratisaṃvedī /
body.translated_text: If then one obtains the fundamental first, second, and third <s>dhyānas</s> — one inevitably also obtains the preliminary stage of the first <s>dhyāna</s>, the access concentration. Relying on that, one examines one's own arisen mind — whether it is with attachment or

body.text: sa yadā styānamiddhanivaraṇena cittaṃ nivṛtaṃ bhavaty adhyātmam saṃśamayatas tadānyatamānyatamena prasadanīyenālambanena saṃdarśayati samādāpayati samuttejayati saṃpraharṣayati / tenāhābhipramodayaṃś (

children.translated_text: <s>Śbh</s> II 104
) the mind."

body.translated_text: When the mind is covered by the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor while one is calming [the mind] internally, then by means of some gladdening object, one inspires, encourages, stimulates, and delights [the mind]. Therefore it says: "Gladdening

body.text: yadā punar auddhatyanivaraṇena kaukṛtyanivaraṇena nivṛtaṃ paśyaty abhisaṃpragṛhṇatas tadānyatamānyatamena prasadanīyenālambanena saṃdarśayaty adhyātmam avasthāpayati śamayati samādhatte / tenāha samādadhaṃś cittam /
body.translated_text: When one sees [the mind] covered by the hindrance of restlessness or the hindrance of remorse while one is restraining [it], then by means of some calming object, one inspires, establishes internally, calms, and concentrates [the mind]. Therefore it says: "Concentrat-

body.text: yadā ca tac cittam āsevanānvayād bhāvanānvayād bahulīkārānvayān nivaraṇasamudācārād dūrīkṛtaṃ bhavati nivaraṇebhyo viśodhitam / tenāha vimocayaṃś cittam āśvasan "vimocayaṃś cittam āśvasimī"ti śikṣate /
body.translated_text: ing the mind." When that mind, through the continuity of practice, the continuity of cultivation, and the continuity of repeated application, has been distanced from the arising of hindrances and purified from the hindrances — therefore it says: "Liberating the mind while breathing in, one trains: 'I breathe in liberating the mind,'"

body.text: tasya nivaraṇebhyo vimuktacetaso mārgabhāvanāyā āntarāyikebhyo 'nuśayā avaśiṣṭā bhavanti prahātavyāḥ / sa teṣāṃ prahāṇāya mārgaṃ saṃmukhīkaroti / yaduta saṃskārānityatām eva sādhu ca suṣṭhu ca yoniśaḥ pratyaveksate / tenāha anityānudarśī /
body.translated_text: For one whose mind is freed from hindrances, there remain the latent tendencies that are obstructive to the cultivation of the path, which are to be abandoned. For their abandonment, one directs oneself toward the path — namely, one thoroughly and properly, in a methodical way, [contemplates] the impermanence of formations.

body.text: tena ca pūrvaṃ prathamadvitīyatṛtīyadhyānasanniśrayeṇānāgamyasaṃniśrayeṇa vā punaḥ śamathayogaḥ kṛtaḥ / etarhy anityānudarśī vipaśyanāyāṃ yogaṃ karoti / evam asya tac cittaṃ śamathavipaśyanāparibhāvitaṃ dhātuṣu vimucyate yadutānuśayebhyaḥ /
body.translated_text: And previously, relying on the first, second, or third <s>dhyāna</s>, or relying on the access concentration, one has practiced the yoga of <s>śamatha</s> (calm abiding). Now, contemplating impermanence, one practices the yoga of <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight). Thus one's mind is cultivated by <s>śamatha</s> and <s>vipaśyanā</s> —

body.text: katame dhātavaḥ / yaś ca prahāṇadhātur yaś ca virāgadhātur yaś ca nirodhadhātuḥ / tatra sarvasaṃskārāṇāṃ darśanaprahātavyānāṃ prahāṇāt (

children.translated_text: <s>Śbh</s> II 106

children.text: ) prahāṇadhātuḥ / sarvasaṃskārāṇāṃ bhāvanāprahātavyānāṃ prahāṇād virāgadhātuḥ / sarvopadhinirodhān nirodhadhātuḥ / sa evaṃ trīn dhātuñ śāntato manasikurvan kṣemata ārogyataḥ śamathavipaśyanāṃ bhāvayati / yenāsyāsevanānvayād bhāvanānvayād bahulīkārānvayād avaśiṣṭebhyo bhāvanāprahātavyebhyaḥ kleśebhyaś cittaṃ vimucyate / tenāha prahāṇānudarśī, virāgānudarśī, nirodhānudarśy āśvasan "nirodhānudarśy āśvasimī"ti śikṣate /
children.translated_text: the element of abandonment. Through the abandonment of all formations that are to be abandoned by cultivation, the element of dispassion. Through the cessation of all bases of existence, the element of cessation. One thus attending to the three elements as peace, as safety, as health, cultivates <s>śamatha</s> (calm abiding) and <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight). By which, through repeated practice, cultivation, and frequent application, the mind is liberated from the remaining afflictions that are to be abandoned by cultivation. Therefore it is said: contemplating abandonment, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation — breathing in, one trains thus: "I shall breathe in contemplating cessation."

body.translated_text: What are the elements? The element of abandonment, the element of dispassion, and the element of cessation. Therein, from the abandonment of all formations to be abandoned by seeing,

body.text: evam ayaṃ darśanabhāvanāprahātavyeṣu kleśeṣu prahīṇeṣv arhan bhavati kṣīṇāsravaḥ, nāsty asyāta uttari karaṇīyam / bhavati kṛto 'sya paricayaḥ / ayam asyocyate ṣoḍaśākāraḥ paricayaḥ / yaś cāyaṃ pañcavidhaḥ paricaya iyam asyocyata ānāpānasmṛtiḥ /
body.translated_text: Thus this one, when the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing and by cultivation have been abandoned, becomes an <s>arhat</s> (worthy one), one whose <s>āśravas</s> (defilements) are destroyed — there is nothing further to be done. One's familiarity is complete. This is called the sixteenfold familiarization. And this fivefold familiarization — this is called one's <s>ānāpānasmṛti</s> (mindfulness of breathing).

body.text: yatra vitarkacaritaḥ pudgalaḥ prayujyamānaḥ priyārohatayā prayujyate / savyāpāraṃ caitad ālambanaṃ savyākṣepam adhyātmaṃ pratyātmam āsannāsannaṃ, yenāsya tatra prayujyamānasya yo vitarkasaṃkṣobhaḥ sa na bhavati / tvaritatvaritaṃ ca cittam ālambane saṃtiṣṭhate, abhiramate / idaṃ pañcamaṃ vitarkacaritasya pudgalasya caritaviśodhanam ālambanam //
body.translated_text: Herein a person of discursive temperament, when practicing, practices with delight in the practice. And this object is engrossing, involving, close at hand, internal and personal — by which, when one practices with it, the disturbance of discursive thinking does not arise; and the mind quickly settles on and delights in the object. This is the fifth object for purifying the conduct of a person of discursive temperament.

body.text:
-II-3-c Ms.77a7R, Sh. 237-6, W.*91-24, P.111a3, D.91a3, N.96a2, Co.96a6, Ch.433c1
tatra kauśalyālambanaṃ katamat / tadyathā skandhakauśalyaṃ dhātukauśalyam āyatanakauśalyaṃ pratītyasamutpādakauśalyaṃ sthānāsthānakauśalyam //
body.translated_text: -II-3-c — Therein, what is the object of skill? Namely: skill in the <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates), skill in the <s>dhātus</s> (elements), skill in the <s>āyatanas</s> (sense-bases), skill in <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination), and skill in what is possible and impossible.

body.text:
-II-3-c-(1) Ms.77a8M, Sh.237-9, P.111a4, D.91a4, N.96a3, Co.96a7, Ch.433c4
tatra katame skandhāḥ, katamat skandhakauśalyam / āha / pañca skandhāḥ rūpaskandho vedanāskandhaḥ saṃjñāskandhaḥ saṃskāraskandho vijñānaskandhaś ca /
body.translated_text: -II-3-c-(1) — Therein, what are the <s>skandhas</s>? What is skill in the <s>skandhas</s>? It is said: There are five <s>skandhas</s> — the aggregate of form (<s>rūpaskandha</s>), the aggregate of feeling (<s>vedanāskandha</s>), the aggregate of perception (<s>saṃjñāskandha</s>), the aggregate of volitional formations (<s>saṃskāraskandha</s>), and the aggregate of consciousness (<s>vijñānaskandha</s>).

body.text: tatra rūpaskandhaḥ katamaḥ / yat kiñcid rūpaṃ sarvaṃ tac catvāri mahābhūtāni catvāri mahābhūtāny upādāya / tat punar atītānāgatapratyutpannam ādhyātmikaṃ vā bāhyaṃ vaudārikaṃ vā sūkṣmaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā praṇītaṃ vā dūre vāntike vā /
body.translated_text: Therein, what is the aggregate of form? Whatever form there is — all of that is the four great elements and that which depends on the four great elements. That is further [classified as] past, future, and present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near.

body.text: tatra vedanāskandhaḥ katamaḥ / sukhavedanīyaṃ vā sparśaṃ pratītya, duḥkhavedanīyaṃ vā, aduḥkhāsukhavedanīyaṃ vā / ṣaḍ vedanākāyāś cakṣuḥsaṃsparśajā vedanā śrotraghrāṇajihvākāyamanaḥsaṃsparśajā vedanā /
body.translated_text: Therein, what is the aggregate of feeling? Dependent on a contact that is to be felt as pleasant, or to be felt as painful, or to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant — there are six bodies of feeling: feeling born of eye-contact, feeling born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.

body.text: tatra saṃjñāskandhaḥ katamaḥ / tadyathā sanimittasaṃjñā, animittasaṃjñā, parīttasaṃjñā, mahadgatasaṃjñā, apramāṇasaṃjñā, nāsti kiñcid ity ākiñcanyāyatanasaṃjñā / ṣaṭ saṃjñākāyāś cakṣuḥsaṃsparśajā saṃjñā śrotraghrāṇajihvākāyamanaḥsaṃsparśajā saṃjñā /
body.translated_text: Therein, what is the aggregate of perception? Such as: perception with a sign, perception without a sign, limited perception, expansive perception, unlimited perception, and the perception of the sphere of nothingness — "There is nothing." There are six bodies of perception: perception born of eye-contact, perception born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.

body.text:
saṃskāraskandhaḥ katamaḥ / ṣaṭ cetanākāyāś cakṣuḥsaṃsparśajā cetanā, śrotraghrāṇajihvākāyamanaḥsaṃsparśajā cetanā / vedanāṃ ca saṃjñāṃ ca sthāpayitvā ye tadanye caitasikā dharmāḥ /
tatra vijñānaskandhaḥ katamaḥ / yac cittaṃ mano vijñānam / te punaḥ ṣaḍ vijñānakāyāḥ / cakṣurvijñānaṃ śrotraghrāṇajihvākāyamanovijñānam /
body.translated_text: What is the aggregate of volitional formations? There are six bodies of volition: volition born of eye-contact, volition born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact — and, setting aside feeling and perception, whatever other mental factors there are. Therein, what is the aggregate of consciousness? That which is mind (<s>citta</s>), mentation (<s>manas</s>), consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>). Those are the six bodies of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness.

body.text: sā caiṣā vedanā saṃjñā saṃskāras tac caitad vijñānam atītānāgatapratyutpannam ādhyātmikaṃ vā bāhyaṃ veti vistareṇa pūrvavat / ima ucyante skandhāḥ /
body.translated_text: And this feeling, perception, volitional formations, and this consciousness — [all are classified as] past, future, and present; internal or external — and so on in detail as before. These are called the <s>skandhas</s>.

body.text: skandhakauśalyaṃ katamat / ya etān yathoddiṣṭān dharmāN nānātmakatayā (

children.translated_text: Śbh II 110

children.text: ) ca jānāti bahvātmakatayā ca, na ca tataḥ param upalabhate vikalpayati vā / idam ucyate samāsataḥ skandhakauśalyam /
children.translated_text: and in their multiplicity, and does not apprehend or conceptualize anything beyond that — this is called, in summary, skill in the <s>skandhas</s>.

body.translated_text: What is skill in the <s>skandhas</s>? That one knows these <s>dharmas</s> as enumerated, in their diversity

body.text: tatra katamā nānātmakatā skandhānām / anya eva rūpaskandho 'nyo vedanāskandha evam anyo yāvad vijñānaskandhaḥ / iyaṃ nānātmakatā /
body.translated_text: Therein, what is the diversity of the <s>skandhas</s>? The aggregate of form is one thing, the aggregate of feeling is another — thus each is different, up to the aggregate of consciousness. This is the diversity.

body.text: tatra katamā bahvātmakatā / yo rūpaskandho 'nekavidho bahunānāprakāraḥ, bhūtabhautikabhedenātītānāgatapratyutpannādikena ca prakārabhedena / iyam ucyata anekātmakatā rūpaskandhasya / evam avaśiṣṭānām skandhānāṃ yathāyogaṃ veditavyam /
body.translated_text: Therein, what is the multiplicity? The aggregate of form is of many kinds, of many diverse types — by the division into primary and derived [elements], and by the divisions of past, future, present, and so forth. This is called the multiplicity of the aggregate of form. Likewise for the remaining <s>skandhas</s>, it should be understood as appropriate.

body.text: kiṃ ca na tasmāt param upalabhate vikalpayati / skandhamātram upalabhate vastumātram / no tu skandhavyatirekeṇātmānam upalabhate nityadhruvam avipariṇāmadharmakam / nāpy ātmīyaṃ, kiṃcid idaṃ nopalabhate, na vikalpayati tasmāt pareṇa //
body.translated_text: And what does one not apprehend or conceptualize beyond that? One apprehends merely the aggregates, merely the things — but one does not apprehend, apart from the aggregates, a self that is permanent, stable, of unchanging nature. Nor does one apprehend or conceptualize anything belonging to a self, anything at all beyond that.

body.text:
-11-3-0(2) Ms.77b6L, Sh.244-12, P.112a6, D.92a3, N.97a2, Co.97a5, Ch.434a3
tatra katame dhātavaḥ / katamad dhātukauśalyam / āha / aṣṭādaśa dhātavaḥ / cakṣurdhātū rūpadhātuś cakṣurvijñānadhātuḥ śrotradhātuḥ śabdadhātuḥ śrotravijñānadhātur ghrāṇadhātur gandhadhātur ghrāṇavijñānadhātur jihvādhātū rasadhātur jihvāvijñānadhātuḥ kāyadhātuḥ spraṣṭavyadhātuḥ kāyavijñānadhātur manodhātur dharmadhātur manovijñānadhātuḥ / ima ucyante dhātavaḥ /
body.translated_text: -II-3-c-(2) — Therein, what are the <s>dhātus</s>? What is skill in the <s>dhātus</s>? It is said: There are eighteen <s>dhātus</s> (elements): the eye-element, the form-element, the eye-consciousness-element; the ear-element, the sound-element, the ear-consciousness-element; the nose-element, the smell-element, the nose-consciousness-element; the tongue-element, the taste-element, the tongue-consciousness-element; the body-element, the tangible-element, the body-consciousness-element; the mind-element, the <s>dharma</s>-element, the mind-consciousness-element. These are called the <s>dhātus</s>.

body.text: tatra katamad dhātukauśalyam / yat punar etān aṣṭādaśa dharmān svakāt svakād dhātoḥ svakasvakād bījāt svakasvakād gotrāj jāyante nirvartante prādurbhavantīti jānāti rocayann upanidhyāti / idam ucyate dhātukauśalyam / yad aṣṭādaśānāṃ dharmāṇām svakasvakād dhātoḥ pravṛttiṃ jānāti tad evam sati hetupratyayakauśalyam etad yaduta dhātukauśalyam //
body.translated_text: Therein, what is skill in the <s>dhātus</s>? That one knows that these eighteen <s>dharmas</s> arise, are produced, and come into being from their own respective element, from their own respective seed, from their own respective lineage — and knowing this, one approves and contemplates it. This is called skill in the <s>dhātus</s>. That one knows the functioning of the eighteen <s>dharmas</s> from their own respective element — this being so, this is skill in cause and condition — namely, skill in the <s>dhātus</s>.

body.text:
-II-3-c-(3) Ms.77b8M, Sh.245-12, P.112b3, D.92a7, N.97a6, Co.97b1, Ch.434a11
tatra katamāny āyatanāni / katamad āyatanakauśalyam / āha / dvādaśāyatanāni, cakṣurāyatanam, rūpāyatanam, śrotrāyatanam, śabdāyatanam, ghrāṇāyatanam, gandhāyatanam, jihvāyatanam, rasāyatanam, kāyāyatanam, spraṣṭavyāyatanam, mana-āyatanam, dharmāyatanaṃ ca / imāny ucyanta āyatanāni /
body.translated_text: -II-3-c-(3) — Therein, what are the <s>āyatanas</s>? What is skill in the <s>āyatanas</s>? It is said: There are twelve <s>āyatanas</s> (sense-bases): the eye sense-base, the form sense-base, the ear sense-base, the sound sense-base, the nose sense-base, the smell sense-base, the tongue sense-base, the taste sense-base, the body sense-base, the tangible sense-base, the mind sense-base, and the <s>dharma</s> sense-base. These are called the <s>āyatanas</s>.

body.text: katamad āyatanakauśalyam / tatra cakṣur adhipatī rūpāṇy ālambanaṃ cakṣurvijñānasya sasaṃprayogasyotpattaye, samanantaraniruddhaṃ ca manaḥ samanantarapratyayaḥ / tatra śrotram adhipatiḥ śabda ālambanaṃ samanantaraniruddhaṃ ca manaḥ samanantarapratyayaḥ śrotravijñānasya sasaṃprayogasyotpattaye / evaṃ yāvan manaḥsamanantaraṃ tajjo manaskāro 'dhipatipratyayo dharma ālambanaṃ manovijñānasya sasaṃprayogasyotpattaye, iti tribhiḥ pratyayaiḥ samanantarapratyayena ālambanapratyayena adhipatipratyayena ca ṣaṇṇāṃ vijñānakāyānāṃ pravṛttir bhavati sasaṃprayogāṇām iti / yad evam ādhyātmikabāhyeṣv āyataneṣu pratyayakauśalyam / idam ucyata āyatanakauśalyam //
body.translated_text: What is skill in the <s>āyatanas</s>? Therein, the eye is the dominant condition, forms are the object-condition, for the arising of eye-consciousness together with its associated [mental factors]; and the immediately preceding mind that has ceased is the immediate condition. Therein, the ear is the dominant condition, sound is the object-condition, and the immediately preceding mind that has ceased is the immediate condition for the arising of ear-consciousness together with its associated [factors]. Likewise up to: the mind together with the mental engagement born from it is the dominant condition, <s>dharmas</s> are the object-condition, for the arising of mind-consciousness together with its associated [factors]. Thus by three conditions — the immediate condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition — the six bodies of consciousness, together with their associated [factors], function. That one thus has skill in conditions regarding the internal and external <s>āyatanas</s> — this is called skill in the <s>āyatanas</s>.

body.text:
-II-3-c-(4) Ms.78a3L, Sh.247-10, P.113a3, D.92b5, N.97b5, Co.97b7, Ch.434a22
tatra katamaḥ pratītyasamutpādaḥ, katamat pratītyasamutpādakauśalyam / āha / avidyāpratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ, saṃskārapratyayaṃ vijñānam, vijñānapratyayaṃ nāmarūpam / vistareṇa yāvat / evam asya kevalasya mahato duḥkhaskandhasya samudayo bhavati / ayam ucyate pratītyasamutpādaḥ /
body.translated_text: -II-3-c-(4) — Therein, what is <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s> (dependent origination)? What is skill in <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>? It is said: Conditioned by <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), <s>saṃskāras</s> (volitional formations) [arise]; conditioned by <s>saṃskāras</s>, <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness) [arises]; conditioned by <s>vijñāna</s>, <s>nāmarūpa</s> (name-and-form) [arises] — and so on in detail — thus the origination of this entire great mass of suffering comes about. This is called <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>.

body.text: yat punar dharmā eva dharmān abhispandayanti dharmā eva dharmān parispandayanti / saṃskārā eva dharmāṇām āhārakāḥ, te ca hetusamutpannatvāt (

children.translated_text: Śbh II 114

children.text: ) pratītyasamutpannatvād abhūtvā bhavanti bhūtvā ca prativigacchanti / tasmād anityā ete saṃskārāḥ / ye punar anityās te jātidharmāṇo jarādharmāṇo vyādhidharmāṇo maraṇadharmāṇaḥ śokaparidevaduḥkhadaurmanasyopāyāsadharmāṇaḥ / te jarādharmitvād yāvad upāyāsadharmitvād duḥkhāḥ / ye vā punar duḥkhā, asvatantrā, durbalās ta anātmāna iti / yad ebhir ākāraiḥ pratītyasamutpanneṣu dharmeṣv anityajñānam, duḥkhajñānam, nairātmyajñānam / idam ucyate pratītyasamutpādakauśalyam //
children.translated_text: arisen dependently — not having been, they come to be; and having been, they pass away. Therefore these formations are impermanent. Those that are impermanent are subject to birth, subject to aging, subject to illness, subject to death, subject to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, dejection, and despair. Being subject to aging and so forth up to being subject to despair, they are suffering. Those that are suffering are without self-mastery, weak — they are non-self. That one has knowledge of impermanence, knowledge of suffering, and knowledge of non-self with respect to <s>dharmas</s> that have arisen dependently, by these aspects — this is called skill in <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>.

body.translated_text: Furthermore, <s>dharmas</s> alone cause <s>dharmas</s> to move; <s>dharmas</s> alone cause <s>dharmas</s> to stir. Formations alone are the nourishers of <s>dharmas</s>; and since they are arisen from causes,

body.text:
-II-3-c-(5) Ms.78a6L, Sh.249-3, P.113b5, D.93a5, N.98a6, Co.98a7, Ch.434b6
sthānāsthānakauśalyaṃ punaḥ pratītyasamutpādakauśalyaviśeṣa eva veditavyam //
body.translated_text: -II-3-c-(5) — Skill in what is possible and impossible should be understood as a special case of skill in <s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>.

body.text: tatrāyaṃ viśeṣaḥ / sthānāsthānakauśalyenāviṣamahetukatāṃ jānāti / asti kuśalākuśalānāṃ karmaṇāṃ phalavipākaḥ / kuśalānāṃ punar iṣṭaḥ phalavipākaḥ / akuśalānām aniṣṭa iti / yad evaṃ jñānam idam ucyate sthānāsthānakauśalyam /
body.translated_text: Therein, this is the distinction: through skill in what is possible and impossible, one knows the non-uneven causality [of things]. There is a ripening result of wholesome and unwholesome actions — the ripening result of wholesome [actions] is desirable, the ripening result of unwholesome [actions] is undesirable. That one thus has knowledge — this is called skill in what is possible and impossible.

body.text: tac caitat pañcasthānakauśalyaṃ samāsataḥ svalakṣaṇakauśalyaṃ bhavati sāmānyalakṣaṇakauśalyaṃ ca / tatra skandhakauśalyena svalakṣaṇakauśalyam ākhyātam avaśiṣṭaiḥ sāmānyalakṣaṇakauśalyam / idam ucyate kauśalyālambanam //
body.translated_text: And this fivefold skill, in summary, constitutes skill in own-characteristics and skill in general characteristics. Therein, through skill in the <s>skandhas</s>, skill in own-characteristics has been explained; through the remaining [skills], skill in general characteristics [has been explained]. This is called the object of skill.

body.text:
-II-3-d-(1) Ms.78b1R, Sh.249-12, W.*91-33, P.114a1, D.93b1, N.98b2, Co.98b3, Ch.434b14
tatra kleśaviśodhanam ālambanaṃ katamat / āha / adhobhūmīnām audārikatvam uparibhūmīnāṃ śāntatvaṃ ca / tadyathā kāmadhātau prathamadhyānasya evaṃ yāvan naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanasya /
body.translated_text: -II-3-d-(1) — Therein, what is the object for purifying the afflictions? It is said: The coarseness of the lower realms and the peacefulness of the higher realms — such as, relative to the desire-realm, the first <s>dhyāna</s>, and so on up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

body.text: tatra katamā audārikatā / audārikatā dvividhā / svabhāvaudārikatā saṃkhyaudārikatā ca /
body.translated_text: Therein, what is coarseness? Coarseness is twofold: intrinsic coarseness and quantitative coarseness.

body.text: tatra svabhāvaudārikatā kāmadhātāv api pañcaskandhāḥ saṃvidyante prathame tu dhyāne / ye kāmāvacarās te sādīnavatarāś ca duḥkhavihāratarāś ca, (

children.translated_text: Śbh II 116

children.text: ) alpakāvasthāyitarāś ca, hīnatarāḥ pratikruṣṭatarāś ca / iyam eṣām svabhāvaudārikatā / prathame tu dhyāne na tathā tena te śāntatarāḥ praṇītatarā ity ucyante /
children.translated_text: more transient, more inferior, and more contemptible. This is their intrinsic coarseness. But in the first <s>dhyāna</s> it is not so; therefore those are called more peaceful and more excellent.

body.translated_text: Therein, what is intrinsic coarseness? In the desire-realm too there exist the five <s>skandhas</s>, and in the first <s>dhyāna</s> too. But those belonging to the desire-realm are more disadvantageous, more of the nature of suffering,

body.text: tatra saṃkhyaudārikatā katamā / kāmāvacaro rūpaskandhaḥ prabhūtataraḥ parijñeyaḥ prahātavya evaṃ yāvad vijñānaskandhaḥ / iyam ucyate saṃkhyaudārikatā / evam uparimāsu bhūmiṣu svabhāvaudārikatā saṃkhyaudārikatā ca yathāyogaṃ veditavyāḥ /
body.translated_text: Therein, what is quantitative coarseness? The aggregate of form belonging to the desire-realm is more abundant — [it is] to be fully understood, to be abandoned — and likewise up to the aggregate of consciousness. This is called quantitative coarseness. Likewise in the higher realms, intrinsic coarseness and quantitative coarseness should be understood as appropriate.

body.text: iyaṃ tūparimāsu bhūmiṣu yāvad ākiṃcanyāyatanāt tadaudārikatā veditavyāḥ, sarvā adharimā bhūmayo duḥkhavihāratarāś ca alpāyuṣkatarāś ca / naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanaṃ punaḥ śāntam eva, upari śreṣṭhatarāyā bhūmer abhāvāt /
body.translated_text: But in the higher realms, up to the sphere of nothingness, that coarseness should be understood — all lower realms are more of the nature of suffering and of shorter lifespan. The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, however, is peaceful only, due to the absence of a superior realm above it.

body.text: tatra samāsata ādīnavārtha audārikatārthaḥ / yasyāṃ yasyāṃ bhūmau prabhūtataram ādīnavaṃ bhavati, sā ādīnavata audārikety ucyate /
body.translated_text: Therein, in summary, the meaning of disadvantage is the meaning of coarseness. Whatever stage has a greater abundance of disadvantage, that stage is called 'coarse' from the standpoint of disadvantage.

body.text: yasyāṃ tu yasyāṃ bhūmāv alpataram ādīnavaṃ bhavati, sā ādīnavataḥ śāntety ucyate / idaṃ laukikānāṃ laukikena mārgeṇa kleśaviśodhanam ālambanam, tathāpi tasyādharimāṃ bhūmim ādīnavataḥ paśyataḥ / rogataḥ, ayogakṣemataḥ, uparimāṃ ca bhūmiṃ śāntataḥ / ya adhobhūmikāḥ kleśā yāvad ākiṃcanyāyatanabhūmikāḥ kāmadhātum upādāya te prahīyante / na tv atyantataḥ prahīyante / te punar eva te pratisaṃdhikā bhavanti //
body.translated_text: But whatever stage has a lesser amount of disadvantage, that stage is called 'peaceful' from the standpoint of disadvantage. This is the worldly object for the purification of afflictions by the worldly path: indeed, seeing the lower stage as disadvantageous — as a disease, as insecurity — and the upper stage as peaceful, the afflictions pertaining to the lower stages, from the desire realm (<s>kāmadhātu</s>) up to the stage of the sphere of nothingness (<s>ākiṃcanyāyatana</s>), are abandoned. But they are not abandoned definitively. They again become the [basis for] re-linking [in rebirth]. //

body.text:
-II-3-d-(2)-i Ms.78b6M, Sh.251-11, P.114b6, D.94a3, N.99a4, Co.99a4, Ch.434c9
lokottareṇa vā punar mārgeṇa kleśaviśodhanam ālambanaṃ caturvidhaṃ tadyathā duḥkhasatyaṃ samudayasatyaṃ nirodhasatyaṃ mārgasatyaṃ ca /
body.translated_text: The object for the purification of afflictions by the supramundane path is fourfold, namely: the truth of suffering (<s>duḥkhasatya</s>), the truth of origination (<s>samudayasatya</s>), the truth of cessation (<s>nirodhasatya</s>), and the truth of the path (<s>mārgasatya</s>).

body.text: tatra duḥkhasatyaṃ katamat / tadyathā jātir duḥkhaṃ jarā duḥkhaṃ vyādhir maraṇam apriyasaṃprayogaḥ priyavinābhāva icchāvighātaś ca / saṃkṣepataḥ pañcopādānaskandhā duḥkham /
body.translated_text: Therein, what is the truth of suffering? Namely: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness, death, association with the unpleasant, separation from the pleasant, and frustration of desire — all are suffering. In brief, the five aggregates of clinging (<s>pañcopādānaskandha</s>) are suffering.

body.text: tatra samudaya āryasatyaṃ tṛṣṇā paunarbhavikī nandīrāgasahagatā tatratatrābhinandinī /
body.translated_text: Therein, the noble truth of origination is craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>) — that which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and passion, finding pleasure here and there.

body.text: tatra nirodha āryasatyaṃ yad asyā eva tṛṣṇāyā aśeṣaprahāṇam /
body.translated_text: Therein, the noble truth of cessation is the complete abandonment of that very craving.

body.text: mārgasatyam āryāṣṭāṅgo mārgaḥ /
body.translated_text: The truth of the path is the noble eightfold path (<s>āryāṣṭāṅga mārga</s>).

body.text: tatra kṛṣṇapakṣaṃ śuklapakṣaṃ copādāya hetuphalavyavasthānena catuḥsatyavyavasthānam / tatra duḥkhasatyaṃ phalam / samudayasatyaṃ hetuḥ / nirodhasatyaṃ phalam / mārgasatyaṃ hetuḥ prāptaye sparśanāyai /
body.translated_text: Therein, based on the dark side and the bright side, the determination of the four truths is by the arrangement of cause and effect. Therein, the truth of suffering is the effect. The truth of origination is the cause. The truth of cessation is the effect. The truth of the path is the cause — for the attainment and contact [of cessation].

body.text: tatra duḥkhasatyaṃ vyādhisthānīyaṃ tat prathamataḥ parijñeyam / samudayasatyaṃ vyādhinidānasthānīyaṃ tac cāntaraṃ parivarjayitavyam / nirodhasatyam ārogyasthānīyaṃ tac ca sparśayitavyaṃ sākṣātkartavyam / mārgasatyaṃ bhaiṣajyasthānīyaṃ tac cāsevitavyaṃ bhāvayitavyaṃ bahulīkartavyam //
body.translated_text: Therein, the truth of suffering is analogous to a disease — that is to be fully understood first. The truth of origination is analogous to the cause of the disease — that is to be secondarily abandoned. The truth of cessation is analogous to health — that is to be contacted and directly realized. The truth of the path is analogous to medicine — that is to be practiced, cultivated, and frequently applied. //

body.text:
-II-3-d-(2)-ii Ms.79a3M, Sh. 253"11, P.115a7, D.94b3, N.99b4, Co.99b3, Ch.434c23
bhūtaṃ caitat tathā avitathā aviparītam aviparyastaṃ duḥkhaṃ duḥkhārthena, yāvan mārgo mārgārthena tasmāt satyam ity ucyate / svalakṣaṇaṃ ca na visaṃvadati / taddarśanāc cāviparītā buddhayaḥ pravartante / tena satyam ity ucyate //
body.translated_text: And this is real, thus, not false, not erroneous, not distorted — suffering in the sense of suffering, and so on up to the path in the sense of the path. Therefore it is called 'truth.' And its own characteristic does not deceive. And from seeing it, non-erroneous cognitions arise. Therefore it is called 'truth.' //

body.text:
-II-3-d-(2)-iii Ms.79a4L, Sh.254-5, P.115b1, D.94b4, N.99b5, Co.99b5, Ch.434c26
kasmāt punar etāny āryāṇām eva satyāni bhavanti / āryā etāni satyāny eva samānāni satyato jānanti paśyanti yathābhūtam / bālās tu na jānanti, na paśyanti yathābhūtam / tasmād āryasatyānīty ucyante / bālānām etad dharmatayā satyaṃ nāvabodhena / āryāṇāṃ tūbhayathā //
body.translated_text: Why are these the truths of the noble ones (<s>ārya</s>) alone? The noble ones know and see these truths as they truly are, as being truths. But the foolish do not know and do not see as they truly are. Therefore they are called noble truths (<s>āryasatya</s>). For the foolish, this is truth by the nature of things, not by understanding. But for the noble ones, it is truth in both ways. //

body.text:
-II-3-d-(2)-iv-(a) Ms.79a4R, Sh.254-10, P.115b4, D.94b6, N.99b7, Co.99b6, Ch.435a1
tatra jātiduḥkham iti jāyamānasya duḥkhā vedanotpadyate kāyikacaitasikī, na tu jātir eva duḥkhaṃ duḥkhanidānam sā evaṃ yāvad icchāvighāto duḥkham iti, icchāvighātanidānaṃ duḥkham utpadyate kāyikacaitasikam, na tv icchāvighāta eva duḥkhaṃ duḥkhanidānaṃ punaḥ sa iti peyālam /
body.translated_text: Therein, 'birth is suffering' means: for one being born, a painful feeling arises, bodily and mental. But birth itself is not suffering — it is a cause of suffering. Likewise, up to 'frustration of desire is suffering' — suffering arises, bodily and mental, caused by the frustration of desire. But frustration of desire itself is not suffering — it is a cause of suffering. Thus the abbreviation.

body.text: saṃkṣepataḥ pañcopādānaskandhā duḥkham ity ebhir jātyādibhiḥ paryāyair duḥkhaduḥkhataiva paridīpitā /
body.translated_text: 'In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering' — by these synonymous expressions beginning with birth and so forth, only the suffering of suffering (<s>duḥkhaduḥkhatā</s>) has been illuminated.

body.text: tatra vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā saṃskāraduḥkhatā cāvaśiṣṭā sā punaḥ pañcopādānaskandhaduḥkhatayā paridīpitā bhavati / tathā hi pañcopādānaskandhās trivedanāparigatās te tathoktāyā duḥkhaduḥkhatāyā bhājanabhūtāḥ / yā ca noktā vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā saṃskāraduḥkhatā ca sāpy eṣv eva draṣṭavyā /
body.translated_text: Therein, the suffering of change (<s>vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā</s>) and the suffering of conditioned existence (<s>saṃskāraduḥkhatā</s>) remain — those are illuminated by the statement about the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging. For the five aggregates of clinging encompass the three feelings, and they are the receptacle of the aforementioned suffering of suffering. And the unmentioned suffering of change and suffering of conditioned existence are also to be seen within those very [aggregates].

body.text: kena punaḥ kāraṇena bhagavatā duḥkhaduḥkhataiva parikīrtitā svaśabdena, vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā saṃskāraduḥkhatā punaḥ paryāyeṇa / tathā hi duḥkhaduḥkhatāyām āryāṇāṃ bālānāṃ ca tulyā duḥkhatābuddhiḥ pravartate / saṃvejikā atyarthaṃ duḥkhaduḥkhatā pūrvam akṛtaprajñānām evaṃ ca deśyamāne sukham avatāro bhavati satyeṣu vineyānām //
body.translated_text: For what reason has the <s>Bhagavān</s> proclaimed the suffering of suffering by its own name, but the suffering of change and the suffering of conditioned existence only by implication? Because with respect to the suffering of suffering, the cognition of suffering is equal for both noble ones and fools. The suffering of suffering is extremely disturbing for those who have not previously cultivated wisdom, and when taught thus, there is an easy entry into the truths for those to be trained. //

body.text:
-II-3-d-(2)-iv-(b) Ms.79a7R, Sh.256-4, P.116a4, D.95a4, N.100a6, Co.99b6, Ch.435a16
tatra trividhāyā duḥkhatāyāḥ kathaṃ vyavasthānaṃ bhavati / yat tāvad duḥkhaṃ jātir duḥkhaṃ yāvad icchāvighāto duḥkham ity anena sādhiṣṭhānā duḥkhā vedanā ākhyātā sā ca duḥkhaduḥkhatā / idaṃ duḥkhaduḥkhatāyā vyavasthānam /
body.translated_text: Therein, how is the determination of the threefold suffering established? The statement 'birth is suffering' up to 'frustration of desire is suffering' — by this, painful feeling with its basis has been explained, and that is the suffering of suffering. This is the determination of the suffering of suffering.

body.text: ye ye vā punar etad vipakṣā dharmās tathā yauvanaṃ jarāyāḥ, vyādher ārogyam, jīvitaṃ maraṇasya, priyasaṃprayogo 'priyasaṃprayogasya, apriyavinābhāvaḥ priyavinābhāvasya, icchāsaṃpattir icchāvighātasya / ye ca duḥkhāyāṃ vedanāyāṃ pravṛttāḥ kleśāḥ sādhiṣṭhānāḥ, ye cārogyādiṣu sukhasthānīyeṣu dharmeṣu tannirjātāyāṃ ca vedanāyāṃ ye pravṛttāḥ kleśāḥ / iyam ucyate vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā /
body.translated_text: Whatever <s>dharmas</s> are the opposites of those — such as youth being the opposite of aging, health the opposite of illness, life the opposite of death, association with the pleasant the opposite of association with the unpleasant, non-separation from the pleasant the opposite of separation from the pleasant, fulfillment of desire the opposite of frustration of desire — and whatever afflictions are engaged with respect to painful feeling with its basis, and whatever afflictions are engaged with respect to <s>dharmas</s> analogous to pleasure such as health and the like, and with respect to the feeling born from them — this is called the suffering of change (<s>vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā</s>).

body.text: tatra sukhā vedanā sādhiṣṭhānā, anityatayā pariṇamantī anyathībhāvādhipateyaṃ duḥkhaṃ vidadhāti / kleśāḥ punaḥ sarvatra pravṛttāḥ paryavasthānata eva duḥkhā bhavanti / vipariṇāmaś ca sa cetasas tasmād vipariṇāmaduḥkhatety ucyate / yathoktaṃ bhagavatā, "avadīrṇavipariṇatena cittena mātṛgrāmasya hastagrahaṇaṃ ce"ti vistaraḥ / yathā coktaṃ "kāmacchandaparyavasthitaḥ kāmacchandaparyavasthānapratyayaṃ tajjaṃ caitasikaṃ duḥkhadaurmanasyaṃ pratisaṃvedayate" / evaṃ vyāpādastyānamiddhauddhatyakaukṛtyavicikitsāparyavasthitas tad anenāgamenāptena paramāptena kleśeṣu duḥkhārtho 'pi labhyate vipariṇāmārtho 'pi / tenocyate kleśavipariṇāmaduḥkhateti, idaṃ vipariṇāmaduḥkhatāyā vyavasthānaṃ /
body.translated_text: Therein, pleasant feeling with its basis, changing through impermanence, brings about suffering through the dominance of becoming-otherwise. And the afflictions engaged everywhere are painful by the very fact of their being afflictive states. And that change is of the mind — therefore it is called the suffering of change. As the <s>Bhagavān</s> has said: 'With a mind torn by change, one grasps the hand of a woman' — and so on in detail. And as it is said: 'One afflicted by the state of sensual desire experiences the mental suffering and anguish that is born of, and conditioned by, the state of sensual desire.' Likewise for the states of ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-remorse, and doubt — by this reliable and supremely reliable scripture, the meaning of suffering is also obtained with respect to the afflictions, and also the meaning of change. Therefore it is called the suffering of affliction-and-change. This is the determination of the suffering of change.

body.text: saṃskāraduḥkhatā punaḥ sarvatragā upādānaskandheṣu / saṃkṣepatas tu yā ca duḥkhaduḥkhatā, yā ca kleśasaṃgṛhītā vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā, yā ca (

children.translated_text: Śbh II 124

children.text: ) sādhiṣṭhānasukhavedanāsaṃgṛhitā tāṃ sthāpayitvā ye tadanye skandhā aduḥkhāsukhasahagatās tannirjātās tadutpattipratyayās tasya cotpannasya sthitibhājanāḥ / iyam ucyate saṃskāraduḥkhatā /
children.translated_text: ) that which is included in pleasant feeling with its basis — whatever other aggregates are accompanied by neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling], born from that, conditions for the arising of that, and receptacles for the persistence of what has arisen — this is called the suffering of conditioned existence.

body.translated_text: The suffering of conditioned existence (<s>saṃskāraduḥkhatā</s>) pervades everything in the aggregates of clinging. In brief, setting aside both the suffering of suffering and the suffering of change included in the afflictions, and

body.text: ye skandhā anityā udayavyayayuktāḥ sopādānās trivedanābhir anuṣaktā dauṣṭhulyopagatā ayogakṣemapatitā avinirmuktā duḥkhaduḥkhatāyā vipariṇāmaduḥkhatāyā asvavaśavartinaś ca / iyam ucyate saṃskāraduḥkhatayā duḥkhatā / idaṃ saṃskāraduḥkhatāyā vyavasthānam /
body.translated_text: Whatever aggregates are impermanent, conjoined with arising and passing away, appropriated, conjoined with the three feelings, attended by the liability to unsatisfactoriness (<s>dauṣṭhulya</s>), fallen into insecurity, not liberated from the suffering of suffering and the suffering of change, and not under their own control — this is called suffering by the suffering of conditioned existence. This is the determination of the suffering of conditioned existence.

body.text: tatra tṛṣṇā prārthanābhilāṣo 'bhinandaneti paryāyāḥ / sā punaḥ prārthanā tribhir mukhaiḥ pravṛttā tadyathā punarbhavaprārthanā, viṣayaprārthanā ca / tatra yā punarbhavaprārthanā sā paunarbhavikī tṛṣṇā / viṣayaprārthanā punar dvividhā / prāpteṣu viṣayeṣu saumanasyādhyavasānasahagatā, aprāpteṣu ca viṣayeṣu saṃyogābhilāṣasahagatā / tatra yā prāpteṣu viṣayeṣu saumanasyādhyavasānasahagatā nandīrāgasahagatety ucyate / yā punar aprāpteṣu viṣayeṣu saṃyogābhilāṣasahagatā tatratatrābhinandinīty ucyate /
body.translated_text: Therein, craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>), longing, and desire are synonyms. That longing, furthermore, operates through three aspects: namely, longing for renewed existence and longing for objects. Therein, the longing for renewed existence is craving that leads to renewed existence (<s>paunarbhavikī tṛṣṇā</s>). The longing for objects is twofold: accompanied by the resolution of elation regarding obtained objects, and accompanied by the desire for union regarding unobtained objects. Therein, that which is accompanied by the resolution of elation regarding obtained objects is called 'craving accompanied by delight and passion' (<s>nandīrāgasahagatā</s>). That which is accompanied by the desire for union regarding unobtained objects is called 'finding pleasure here and there' (<s>tatratatrābhinandinī</s>).

body.text: nirodho 'pi dvividhaḥ / kleśanirodho, upakleśanirodhaś ca /
body.translated_text: Cessation (<s>nirodha</s>) too is twofold: cessation of afflictions (<s>kleśanirodha</s>) and cessation of secondary afflictions (<s>upakleśanirodha</s>).

body.text: mārgo 'pi dvividhaḥ / śaikṣo 'śaikṣaś ca /
body.translated_text: The path (<s>mārga</s>) too is twofold: the path of the learner (<s>śaikṣa</s>) and the path of the one beyond learning (<s>aśaikṣa</s>).

body.text: idam ālambanaṃ kleśaviśodhanaṃ lokottareṇa mārgeṇa veditavyam //
body.translated_text: This object for the purification of afflictions by the supramundane path should be understood thus. //

body.text:
-II-3-e Ms.79b7M, Sh.258-11, P.117b3, D.96a5, N.101b1, Co.101a5, Ch.435b21
tenāha caturvidham ālambanam / vyāpyālambanaṃ caritaviśodhanaṃ kauśalyālambanaṃ kleśaviśodhanaṃ ceti /
body.translated_text: Therefore he has said: the object is fourfold — the pervading object, the temperament-purifying object, the skill-object, and the affliction-purifying object.

body.text:
(II)-A-II-4-a Ms.79b7R, Sh.258-13, W.'91-37, P.117b4, D.96a6, N.101b2, Co.101a6, Ch.435b23
tatrāvavādaḥ katamaḥ / caturvidho 'vavādaḥ / aviparītāvavādaḥ, anupūrvāvavādaḥ, āgamāvavādaḥ, adhigamāvavādaś ca /
body.translated_text: Therein, what is instruction (<s>avavāda</s>)? Instruction is fourfold: non-erroneous instruction, gradual instruction, instruction based on tradition (<s>āgama</s>), and instruction based on realization (<s>adhigama</s>).

body.text: tatrāviparītāvavādaḥ katamaḥ / yad aviparītaṃ dharmam arthaṃ ca deśayati grāhayati bhūtaṃ yad asya niryāti samyagduḥkhakṣayāya duḥkhasyāntakriyāyai / ayam ucyate 'viparītāvavādaḥ /
body.translated_text: Therein, what is non-erroneous instruction? When one teaches and causes to understand the <s>Dharma</s> and the meaning without error — what is true, what leads rightly to the complete destruction of suffering, to making an end of suffering. This is called non-erroneous instruction.

body.text: anupūrvāvavādaḥ katamaḥ / yat kālena dharmaṃ deśayati / uttānottānāni sthānāni tatprathamato grāhayati vācayati, tataḥ paścād gambhīrāṇi, prathamasya vā satyasyābhisamayāya tatprathamato 'vavadate, tataḥ paścāt samudayanirodhamārgasatyasya, prathamasya dhyānasya samāpattaye tatprathamato 'vavadate / tataḥ paścād anyāsāṃ dhyānasamāpattīnām / ayam evaṃbhāgīyo 'nupūrvāvavādo veditavyaḥ / tatrāgamāvavādo yathā tena gurūṇām antikād āgamitaṃ bhavati, gurusthānīyānāṃ yogajñānām ācāryāṇām upādhyāyasya vā, tathāgatasya vā, tathāgataśrāvakasya vā tathaivānenānyūnamadhikaṃ kṛtvā parān avavadate / ayam ucyata āgamāvavādaḥ /
body.translated_text: What is gradual instruction? When one teaches the <s>Dharma</s> at the proper time. One first causes to understand and recite the simpler topics, then afterward the profound ones; one first instructs for the comprehension of the first truth, then afterward for the truth of origination, cessation, and path; one first instructs for the attainment of the first <s>dhyāna</s>, then afterward for the other <s>dhyāna</s> attainments. Gradual instruction of this kind should be understood thus. Therein, instruction based on tradition is when one instructs others exactly as one has received from one's teachers — from those in the position of teachers, from <s>yogins</s> with direct knowledge, from one's preceptor (<s>ācārya</s>) or instructor (<s>upādhyāya</s>), from the <s>Tathāgata</s> or from a disciple of the <s>Tathāgata</s> — without adding or subtracting. This is called instruction based on tradition.

body.text: tatrādhigamāvavādo yathānena te dharmā adhigatā bhavanti / sparśitāḥ sākṣātkṛtā, ekākinā vyavakṛṣṭavihāriṇā / tathaiva pareṣāṃ prāptaye / sparśanāyai sākṣātkriyāyā avavadate / ayam ucyate 'dhigamāvavādaḥ //
body.translated_text: Therein, what is instruction based on realization? When those <s>dharmas</s> have been realized by oneself, contacted, directly experienced, while dwelling alone and in seclusion — one instructs others in exactly the same way for their own attainment, contact, and direct realization. This is called instruction based on realization. //

body.text:
-II-4-b Ms.80a3M, Sh.260-15, P.118a7, D.96b6, N.102a2, Co.101b5, Ch.435c9
asti punaḥ sarvākāraparipūrṇo 'vavādaḥ / sa punaḥ katamaḥ / yas tribhiḥ prātihāryair avavadati / ṛddhiprātihāryeṇa, ādeśanāprātihāryeṇa, anuśāstiprātihāryeṇa /
body.translated_text: There is also instruction complete in every aspect. What is it? When one instructs through three miracles (<s>prātihārya</s>): the miracle of supernatural power (<s>ṛddhiprātihārya</s>), the miracle of mind-reading (<s>ādeśanāprātihārya</s>), and the miracle of instruction (<s>anuśāstiprātihārya</s>).

body.text: ṛddhiprātihāryeṇa, anekavidhaṃ ṛddhiviṣayam upadarśayaty ātmani ca bahumānaṃ janayati pareṣām / yathā tena bahumānajātāḥ śrotrāvadhānena (

children.translated_text: Śbh II 128

children.text: ) yoge manasikāra ādarajātā bhavanti / tatra deśanāprātihāryeṇa cittacaritaā samanveṣya anuśāstiprātihāryeṇa yathendriyam, yathācaritam, yathāvatāraṃ dharmadeśanāṃ deśayati, pratipattau samanuśāsti / tenāyaṃ prātihāryatrayasaṃgṛhītaḥ sarvākāraparipūrṇāvavādo bhavati //
children.translated_text: ) they become engaged in practice and mental attention with eagerness. Therein, through the miracle of mind-reading, having investigated the mental dispositions, and through the miracle of instruction, one teaches the <s>Dharma</s> according to their faculties, according to their temperament, according to their [level of] entry, and instructs them in practice. Therefore, this instruction encompassed by the three miracles is complete in every aspect. //

body.translated_text: Through the miracle of supernatural power, one displays manifold supernatural feats and generates great respect for oneself in others. So that, with respect thus generated, with attentive listening,

body.text:
(II)-A-II-5-a-(1) Ms.80a5M, Sh.261-8, W.*92-4, P.118b5, D.97a2, N.102a6, Co.102a1, Ch.435c20
tatra śikṣā katamā / āha / tisraḥ śikṣāḥ / adhiśīlaṃśikṣā, adhicittam adhiprajñaṃśikṣā /
body.translated_text: Therein, what is the training (<s>śikṣā</s>)? He says: there are three trainings — the training in higher moral conduct (<s>adhiśīlaśikṣā</s>), the training in higher mind (<s>adhicittaśikṣā</s>), and the training in higher wisdom (<s>adhiprajñāśikṣā</s>).

body.text: tatrādhiśīlaṃśikṣā katamā / yathāpi tac "chīlavān viharatī"ti vistareṇa pūrvavat /
body.translated_text: Therein, what is the training in higher moral conduct? As stated in detail previously: 'one dwells endowed with moral conduct.'

body.text: tatrādhicittaṃśikṣā viviktaṃ kāmair viviktaṃ pāpakair akuśalair dharmaiḥ savitarkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ prītisukhaṃ ca prathamaṃ dhyānaṃ yāvac caturthaṃ dhyānam upasaṃpadya viharati / iyam adhicittaṃśikṣā / api khalu sarva ārūpyās tadanyāś ca samādhisamāpattayo 'dhicittaṃśikṣety ucyate / api tu dhyānāni niśritya tatprathamataḥ satyābhisamayo nyāmāvakrāntir bhavati / na tu sarveṇa sarvaṃ vinā dhyānais tasmāt pradhānāni dhyānāni kṛtvādhicittaṃśikṣety uktāni /
body.translated_text: Therein, the training in higher mind: secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome <s>dharmas</s>, with applied thought and sustained thought, born of seclusion, with joy and happiness — one attains and dwells in the first <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation absorption), up to the fourth <s>dhyāna</s>. This is the training in higher mind. Moreover, all the formless [attainments] and other concentrative attainments are also called the training in higher mind. But it is upon the <s>dhyānas</s> that the first realization of the truths (<s>satyābhisamaya</s>) and entry into the fixed course (<s>nyāmāvakrānti</s>) takes place. And it is not entirely possible without the <s>dhyānas</s>. Therefore, making the <s>dhyānas</s> primary, they are called the training in higher mind.

body.text: tatrādhiprajñaṃśikṣā yac caturṣv āryasatyeṣu yathābhūtaṃ jñānaṃ //
body.translated_text: Therein, the training in higher wisdom is the knowledge of the four noble truths (<s>āryasatya</s>) as they really are.

body.text:
-II-5-a-(2) Ms.80a7M, Sh.263-1, P.119a5, D.97a7, N.102b4, Co.102a6, Ch.436a7
kena kāraṇena tisra eva śikṣā na tata ūrdhvam / āha / samādhipratiṣṭhārthena jñānasanniśrayārthena kṛtyakaraṇārthena ca /
body.translated_text: For what reason are there exactly three trainings, not more? He says: for the purpose of establishing concentration, for the purpose of providing a basis for knowledge, and for the purpose of accomplishing the task.

body.text: tatra samādhipratiṣṭhārthenādhiśīlaṃśikṣā / tathā hi śīlaṃ pratiṣṭhāya cittaikāgratāṃ spṛśati cittasamādhim /
body.translated_text: Therein, the training in higher moral conduct is for the purpose of establishing concentration. For indeed, having established oneself in moral conduct, one touches one-pointedness of mind, mental concentration.

body.text: tatra jñānasanniśrayārthenādhicittaṃśikṣā / tathā hi samāhitacittasyaikāgratāsmṛtyā jñeye vastuni yathābhūtaṃ jñānadarśanaṃ pravartate /
body.translated_text: Therein, the training in higher mind is for the purpose of providing a basis for knowledge. For indeed, for one whose mind is concentrated, with the mindfulness of one-pointedness, knowledge and vision of the knowable object operates as it really is.

body.text: tatra kṛtyakaraṇārthenādhiprajñaṃśikṣā / tathā hi suviśuddhena jñānadarśanena kleśaprahāṇam sākṣātkaroti / eṣa hi svārtha etat paramaṃ kṛtyaṃ (

children.translated_text: <s>Śbh</s> II 132

children.text: ) yaduta kleśaprahāṇaṃ tata uttarikaraṇīyaṃ punar nāsti / tenaitās tisra eva śikṣāḥ //
children.translated_text: namely the abandonment of defilements — beyond that, there is nothing further to be done. Therefore, these are exactly three trainings.

body.translated_text: Therein, the training in higher wisdom is for the purpose of accomplishing the task. For indeed, with thoroughly purified knowledge and vision, one directly realizes the abandonment of defilements. This is indeed one's own goal, this is the supreme task,

body.text:
-II-5-a-(3) Ms.80b1M, Sh.263-13, Choi.157-6, P.119b2, D.97b4, N.103a1, Co.102b2, Ch.436a17
kāḥ punar āsāṃ śikṣāṇām ānupūrvī / suviśuddhaśīlasya avipratisāraḥ / avipratisāriṇaḥ prāmodyaṃ prītiḥ prasrabdhiḥ sukham, sukhitasya cittasamādhiḥ samāhitacitto yathābhūtaṃ prajānāti yathābhūtaṃ paśyati / yathābhūtaṃ jānan paśyan nirvidyate nirviṇṇo virajyate / virakto vimucyate / vimukto 'nupādāya parinirvāti / evam imāni śīlāni bhāvitāny agratāyām upanayanti / yadutānupādāya parinirvāṇam / iyam āsāṃ śikṣāṇām ānupūrvī //
body.translated_text: What then is the sequence of these trainings? For one of thoroughly purified moral conduct, there is non-remorse; for one without remorse, there is gladness, joy, tranquility, happiness; for one who is happy, there is mental concentration; for one whose mind is concentrated, one knows as it really is, one sees as it really is; knowing and seeing as it really is, one becomes disenchanted; being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate; being dispassionate, one is liberated; being liberated, without clinging, one attains <s>parinirvāṇa</s> (final liberation). Thus these moral precepts, when cultivated, lead to the highest — namely, <s>parinirvāṇa</s> without clinging. This is the sequence of these trainings.

body.text:
-II-5-a-(4) Ms.80b2R, Sh.264-5, P.119b7, D.97b7, N.103a4, Co.102b5, Ch.436a24
tatra kena kāraṇenādhiśīlaṃ śikṣā adhiśīlam ity ucyate, evam adhicittam adhiprajñam / adhikārārthenādhikārthena ca /
body.translated_text: Therein, for what reason is the training in higher moral conduct called 'higher moral conduct,' and likewise the training in higher mind and higher wisdom? For the purpose of governance and for the purpose of surpassing.

body.text: tatra katham adhikārārthena / adhicittam adhikṛtya yac chīlaṃ sā adhiśīlaṃ śikṣā / adhiprajñam adhikṛtya yaś cittasamādhiḥ, sā adhicittaṃśikṣā / kleśaprahāṇam adhikṛtya yaj jñānaṃ darśanam, sā adhiprajñaṃśikṣā / evam adhikārārthena /
body.translated_text: Therein, how is it for the purpose of governance? The moral conduct that governs the higher mind — that is the training in higher moral conduct. The mental concentration that governs the higher wisdom — that is the training in higher mind. The knowledge and vision that governs the abandonment of defilements — that is the training in higher wisdom. Thus it is for the purpose of governance.

body.text: katham adhikārthena / yā cādhiśīlaṃśikṣā yā cādhicittaṃ yā cādhiprajñaṃśikṣā etāḥ śikṣā asminn eva śāsane, asādhāraṇā ito bāhyaiḥ / evam adhikārthena //
body.translated_text: How is it for the purpose of surpassing? The training in higher moral conduct, the training in higher mind, and the training in higher wisdom — these trainings exist only in this [Buddhist] teaching; they are not shared with those outside [the teaching]. Thus it is for the purpose of surpassing.

body.text:
-II-5-a-(5) Ms.80b4M, Sh.264-16, Choi.*158-5, P.120a5, D.98a4, N.103b1, Co.103a2, Ch.436b3
asti punar adhicittaṃśikṣā yā adhiprajñaṃśikṣāyā āvāhikā, asty adhiprajñaṃśikṣā yā adhicittaṃśikṣāyā āvāhikā / tadyathā āryaśrāvako 'lābhī maulānāṃ dhyānānām, śaikṣo dṛṣṭapadaḥ, tataḥ paścād bhāvanāprahātavyānāṃ (

children.translated_text: <s>Śbh</s> II 134

children.text: ) kleśānāṃ prahāṇāya prayujyamānaḥ smṛtisaṃbodhyaṅgaṃ bhāvayati yāvad upekṣāsaṃbodhyaṅgam / iyam adhiprajñaṃśikṣā adhicittaṃśikṣāyā āvāhikā / adhicittaṃ punaḥ śikṣāṃ adhiprajñāyā āvāhikā pūrvam evoktā /
children.translated_text: being engaged in the abandonment of defilements to be abandoned by cultivation, cultivates the mindfulness factor of awakening (<s>smṛtisaṃbodhyaṅga</s>) up to the equanimity factor of awakening (<s>upekṣāsaṃbodhyaṅga</s>). This training in higher wisdom is conducive to the training in higher mind. The training in higher mind that is conducive to the training in higher wisdom has been stated previously.

body.translated_text: Moreover, there is a training in higher mind that is conducive to the training in higher wisdom, and there is a training in higher wisdom that is conducive to the training in higher mind. Just as the noble disciple who has not attained the fundamental <s>dhyānas</s>, who is a trainee who has seen the path, thereafter

body.text: tatrāsty adhiśīlaṃ śikṣā nādhicittam, nādhiprajñam / asty adhiśīlam adhicittam, nādhiprajñam / na tv asty adhiprajñaṃśikṣā yā vinādhiśīlenādhicittena ca / ato yatrādhiprajñaṃśikṣā tatra tisraḥ śikṣā veditavyāḥ / idaṃ tāvac chikṣāvyavasthānaṃ tatra yoginā yogaprayuktena śikṣitavyam //
body.translated_text: Therein, there exists the training in higher moral conduct without the training in higher mind and without the training in higher wisdom. There exists the training in higher moral conduct together with the training in higher mind, without the training in higher wisdom. But there does not exist the training in higher wisdom without the training in higher moral conduct and the training in higher mind. Therefore, wherever there is the training in higher wisdom, there all three trainings should be understood. This is the classification of the trainings, in which the practitioner engaged in practice should train.

body.text:
-II-5-a-(6) Ms.80b6R, Sh.265-9, P.120b5, D.98b1, N.103b6, Co.103a6 Ch.436b14
tatra trayaḥ pudgalāḥ satyāny abhisamāgacchanti / katame trayaḥ / tadyathā / avītarāgo yadbhūyo vītarāgaḥ, vītarāgaś ca / tatra sarveṇa sarvam avītarāgaḥ satyāny abhisamāgacchan sahasatyābhisamayāt srota-āpanno bhavati / yadbhūyo vītarāgaḥ punaḥ satyāny abhisamāgacchan sahasatyābhisamayāt sakṛdāgāmī bhavati / vītarāgaḥ satyāny abhisamāgacchan sahasatyābhisamayād anāgāmī bhavati //
body.translated_text: Therein, three [types of] persons realize the truths. Which three? Namely: one who has not yet become dispassionate, one who has mostly become dispassionate, and one who has become dispassionate. Therein, one who has in every way not yet become dispassionate, realizing the truths simultaneously with the realization of the truths, becomes a <s>srotāpanna</s> (stream-enterer). One who has mostly become dispassionate, realizing the truths simultaneously with the realization of the truths, becomes a <s>sakṛdāgāmin</s> (once-returner). One who has become dispassionate, realizing the truths simultaneously with the realization of the truths, becomes an <s>anāgāmin</s> (non-returner).

body.text:
-II-5-b Ms.80b7R, Sh.266-1, P.121a1, D.98b4, N.104a2, Co.103b2, Ch.436b19
trīṇīndriyāṇi / anājñātam ājñāsyāmīndriyam ājñendriyam ājñātavata indriyam / eṣām indriyāṇāṃ kathaṃ vyavasthānaṃ bhavati / anabhisamitānāṃ satyānām abhisamayāya prayuktasyānājñātam ājñāsyāmīndriyavyavasthānam / abhisamitavataḥ śaikṣasyājñendriyavyavasthānam / kṛtakṛtyasyāśaikṣasyārhata ājñātāvīndriyavyavasthānam //
body.translated_text: Three faculties: the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (<s>anājñātam ājñāsyāmīndriya</s>), the faculty of knowing (<s>ājñendriya</s>), and the faculty of one who has known (<s>ājñātāvīndriya</s>). How is the classification of these faculties? For one engaged in the realization of truths not yet realized — the classification of the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown.' For a trainee (<s>śaikṣa</s>) who has realized — the classification of the faculty of knowing. For one who has done what was to be done, a beyond-trainee (<s>aśaikṣa</s>), an <s>arhat</s> — the classification of the faculty of one who has known.

body.text:
-II-5-c Ms.81a1L, Sh.267-5, P.121a4, D.98b6, N.104a4, Co.103b3, Ch.436b25
trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni / tadyathā śūnyatā apraṇihitam ānimittam /
body.translated_text: Three gates to liberation (<s>vimokṣamukha</s>): namely, emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>), the signless (<s>ānimitta</s>), and the wishless (<s>apraṇihita</s>).

body.text: eṣāṃ trayāṇāṃ vimokṣamukhānāṃ kathaṃ vyavasthānaṃ bhavati / āha / dvayam idaṃ saṃskṛtam asaṃskṛtaṃ ca /
body.translated_text: How is the classification of these three gates to liberation? He says: this twofold [reality exists] — the conditioned (<s>saṃskṛta</s>) and the unconditioned (<s>asaṃskṛta</s>).

body.text: tatra saṃskṛtaṃ traidhātukapratisaṃyuktāḥ pañca skandhāḥ, asaṃskṛtaṃ punar nirvāṇam / idam ubhayaṃ yac ca saṃskṛtam, yac cāsaṃskṛtam ity ucyate sat / yat punar idam ucyata ātmā vā, sattvo vā, jīvo vā, jantur vā, idam asat /
body.translated_text: Therein, the conditioned is the five <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates) connected with the three realms; the unconditioned is <s>nirvāṇa</s>. Both of these — the conditioned and the unconditioned — are called 'existent.' But what is called 'self,' or 'being,' or 'life-principle,' or 'creature' — this is non-existent.

body.text: tatra saṃskṛte doṣadarśanād ādīnavadarśanād apraṇidhānaṃ bhavati / apraṇidhānāc cāpraṇihitaṃ vimokṣamukhaṃ vyavasthāpyate /
body.translated_text: Therein, from seeing the fault and danger in the conditioned, there is non-wishing. From non-wishing, the wishless (<s>apraṇihita</s>) gate to liberation is established.

body.text: nirvāṇe punas tatra praṇidhānavataḥ praṇidhānaṃ bhavati / śāntadarśanaṃ praṇītadarśanaṃ niḥsaraṇadarśanaṃ ca, niḥsaraṇadarśanāc ca punar ānimittaṃ vimokṣamukhaṃ vyavasthāpyate /
body.translated_text: And in <s>nirvāṇa</s>, for one who has the wishing [directed toward it], there is wishing — seeing it as peaceful, seeing it as sublime, and seeing it as the escape. From seeing it as the escape, the signless (<s>ānimitta</s>) gate to liberation is established.

body.text: tatrāsaty asaṃvidyamāne naiva praṇidhānaṃ nāpraṇidhānaṃ bhavati / tad yathaivāsat tathaivāsad iti jānataḥ paśyataḥ śūnyatāvimokṣamukhaṃ vyavasthāpyate / evaṃ trayāṇāṃ vimokṣamukhānāṃ vyavasthānaṃ bhavati //
body.translated_text: Therein, with regard to what is non-existent and unfound, there is neither wishing nor non-wishing. For one who knows and sees that what is non-existent is indeed just non-existent — the emptiness (<s>śūnyatā</s>) gate to liberation is established. Thus is the classification of the three gates to liberation.

body.text:
(II)-A-II-6-a-(1) Ms.81a3R, Sh.268-12, P.121b3, D.99a4, N.104b2, Co.103b7, Ch.436c11
tatra katame śikṣānulomikā dharmāḥ / āha / daśa śikṣāvilomā dharmāḥ / teṣāṃ pratipakṣeṇa daśa śikṣānulomikā veditavyāḥ /
body.translated_text: Therein, what are the <s>dharmas</s> in conformity with the training? He says: there are ten <s>dharmas</s> that oppose the training. By their antidotes, ten [<s>dharmas</s>] in conformity with the training should be understood.

body.text: tatra katame daśa śikṣāvilomā dharmāḥ / tadyathā mātṛgrāmaḥ śiśur udāravarṇo rañjanīyaḥ śikṣāprayuktasya kulaputrasyādhimātram antarāyakaraḥ paripanthakaḥ / satkāyaparyāpanneṣu saṃskāreṣu niyantiḥ / ālasyam, kausīdyam / satkāyadṛṣṭiḥ kavaḍaṃkārāhāram upādāya rasarāgo lokākhyānakathāsv anekavidhāsu bahunānāprakārāsu citrāsu chandarāgānunayaḥ, dharmacintāyogamanasikārāpakṣālaḥ /
body.translated_text: Therein, what are the ten <s>dharmas</s> that oppose the training? Namely: a woman, young, of excellent complexion, delightful — this is an extreme obstacle and impediment for a son of good family engaged in the training. Clinging to formations included in the individual existence (<s>satkāya</s>). Laziness. Sloth. The view of the individual self (<s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s>). With regard to material food as morsels, attachment to taste. In manifold, various, and elaborate worldly stories, desire-and-passion-and-affection. Detraction from the mental attention of <s>Dharma</s>-reflection and yogic practice.

body.text: sa punaḥ katamaḥ / tadyathā kāṅkṣā vimatir vicikitsā ratneṣu vā satyeṣu vā skandheṣu vā karmaphale vā prahāṇaprayuktasya ca kāyadauṣṭhulyaḥ śaithilikasya śamathavipaśyanāpakṣālamanasikāraḥ styānamiddhena vā cittābhibhavaś cittābhisaṃkṣepaḥ / anvārabdhavīryasya vā kāyikaklamaś caitasikopāyāsaḥ / atilīnavīryasya viśeṣāsaṃprāptiḥ kuśalapakṣaparyādānam / lābhena vā yaśasā vā praśaṃsayā vā anyatamānyatamena vā sukhalavamātratvena nandīsaumanasyam auddhatyam avyupaśama audbilyam utplāvitatvam / satkāyanirodhe nirvāṇa uttrāsaś chambhitatvam / amātrayā bhāṣyaprayogaḥ, atyabhijalpaḥ, dharmyām api kathāṃ kathayatā vigṛhyakathām ārambhānuyogaḥ / pūrvadṛṣṭaśrutānubhūteṣu viṣayeṣv anekavidheṣu bahunānāprakāreṣu cittavisāraś cittākṣepaḥ / acintyeṣu ca sthāneṣu nidhyāyitatvam / ime dharmacintāyogamanasikārāpakṣālā veditavyāḥ / (

children.translated_text: <s>Śbh</s> II 140

body.translated_text: What then are these? Namely: doubt, uncertainty, and vacillation regarding the [Three] Jewels, or the truths, or the aggregates, or the fruits of <s>karma</s>. And for one engaged in abandonment, bodily unsuitability-for-work — slackness, mental attention detrimental to the side of <s>śamatha</s> (calm abiding) and <s>vipaśyanā</s> (insight). Or, the overwhelming and contraction of the mind by sloth-and-torpor. Or, for one whose energy is excessive, bodily fatigue and mental distress. Or, for one whose energy is too lax, non-attainment of distinction and deterioration of the wholesome side. Or, through gain, fame, praise, or any form of even the slightest pleasant [experience], delight, elation, agitation, non-tranquility, excitement, and ebullience. Or, terror and rigidity at the cessation of the individual existence (<s>satkāya</s>), at <s>nirvāṇa</s>. Or, immoderate verbal effort, excessive talk; even while discoursing on a <s>Dharma</s> topic, entering into disputatious debate. Or, mental wandering and distraction toward previously seen, heard, and experienced objects of manifold and various kinds. And brooding over matters that should not be contemplated. These should be understood as detractions from the mental attention of <s>Dharma</s>-reflection and yogic practice.

body.text: dhyānasamāpattisukhāsvādanatā, ānimittaṃ samāpattukāmasya saṃskāranimittānusāritā / spṛṣṭasya śārīrikābhir vedanābhir duḥkhābhir yāvat prāṇahāriṇībhir jīvitaniyantir jīvitāśā, tadāśānugatasya śocanā, klāmyanā, paridevanā / itīme daśa śikṣāvilomā dharmāḥ //
body.translated_text: Relishing the pleasure of <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation) attainments. For one who wishes to attain the signless, being led along by the sign of formations. For one afflicted by painful bodily feelings, even life-threatening ones — clinging to life, the wish for life; and following upon that wish, grief, distress, and lamentation. These are the ten <s>dharmas</s> that oppose the training.

body.text:
-II-6-a-(2) Ms.81b2R, Sh.270-3, P.122a8, D.99b6, N.105a5, Co.104b2, Ch.437a6
katame daśa śikṣāpadānāṃ vilomānāṃ dharmāṇāṃ pratipakṣeṇa śikṣānulomikā bhavanti / tadyathā / aśubhasaṃjñā / anityasaṃjnā / anitye duḥkhasaṃjñā / duḥkhe 'nātmasaṃjñā / āhāre pratikūlasaṃjñā / sarvaloke 'nabhiratisaṃjñā / ālokasaṃjñā / virāgasaṃjñā / nirodhasaṃjñā / maraṇasaṃjñā / itīmā daśa saṃjñā āsevitā bhāvitā bahulīkṛtā daśavidhasya śikṣāparipanthakasya daśānāṃ śikṣāvilomānāṃ dharmāṇāṃ prahāṇāya saṃvartante /
body.translated_text: What are the ten [<s>dharmas</s>] that, as antidotes to the <s>dharmas</s> opposing the training, are in conformity with the training? Namely: the perception of the unpleasant (<s>aśubhasaṃjñā</s>), the perception of impermanence (<s>anityasaṃjñā</s>), the perception of suffering in the impermanent (<s>duḥkhasaṃjñā</s>), the perception of non-self in the suffering (<s>anātmasaṃjñā</s>), the perception of repulsiveness in food (<s>āhāre pratikūlasaṃjñā</s>), the perception of non-delight in the entire world (<s>sarvaloke 'nabhiratisaṃjñā</s>), the perception of light (<s>ālokasaṃjñā</s>), the perception of dispassion (<s>virāgasaṃjñā</s>), the perception of cessation (<s>nirodhasaṃjñā</s>), and the perception of death (<s>maraṇasaṃjñā</s>).
